newsitem.title: JAPAN: BT-MCI merger clouds Japan telecom breakup debate.
newsitem.headline: BT-MCI merger clouds Japan telecom breakup debate.

text.p: The mega-merger of British Telecommunications Plc and MCI Communications Corp has thrown cold water on the argument that Japan's own telecoms giant NTT should be split up to galvanise the domestic market.

The merger has brought to the surface fears that Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp -- Japan's biggest domestic telecommunications carrier -- is lagging behind its foreign rivals, analysts said on Tuesday.
This would encourage the argument that the company should stay intact to strengthen global competitiveness, they said.
"Now, a possibility that Japan's cabinet will order an NTT break-up next year is lessened," said Goldman Sachs (Japan) Corp analyst Eric Gan.

News on Monday that BT of Britain and MCI of the United States will merge in a $20 million deal sent shudders through Japan's telecommunications sector, especially NTT, whose future is still mired in uncertainty.

In February, the government proposed that NTT, which holds 80 percent of Japan's market for domestic telecommunications, be broken up to activate the market. The cabinet put off the decision on the break-up until next year.
In the meantime, progress on all important deregulation involving NTT has ground to a halt.
While mega-carriers spawned by mergers fight for more global market share NTT, barred from entering the international telecommunications market, has been left out of the race.

Also, its foreign ownership is restricted to less than 20 percent, ruling out the possibility of the company joining the race for global mergers and acquisitions. The Japanese government owns two-thirds of NTT's outstanding shares.
"There is nothing to comment on concerning the BT and MCI merger. We have been kept inside an egg shell, barred from the moves of the outer world," one NTT official said.

On Tuesday, NTT's share price closed 10,000 yen ($88) lower at 777,000 yen ($6,876) on fears that the emergence of the world's second largest telecommunications carrier -- the result of the BT-MCI merger -- would narrow NTT's business opportunities abroad in the future, traders said.
The world's biggest telecoms carrier is AT&T Corp of the United States.
"News of the merger elicited scepticism about Japan's telecom deregulation measures," a trader at a large securities company also said.
Meanwhile, analysts also said news of the merger put pressure on Japan's Posts and Telecommunications Ministry to grant NTT a licence to conduct business internationally.

"It is possible that NTT will be allowed international services shortly," said Kiyohisa Ota, analyst at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc. "The government may indicate such a direction by the end of this year."
Posts and Telecommunications Minister Ichiro Hino was quoted as saying on Tuesday that Japan should be careful about breaking up NTT.
"Japan should have a strong operator in the telecommunications field to compete with global mega-carriers," Hino was quoted by a ministry official as telling a news conference. ($1=113 yen)
